source_evidence.location: PDF page 7; printed page 18, Section 2.3 introductory paragraph
source_evidence.anchor: In this section we study Chernoff's inequality, which is sensitive to the magnitudes of p_i
source_evidence.observation: The theorem is introduced as an upper-tail bound adapted to Bernoulli parameters that may be small and need not be equal.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 7; printed page 18, Theorem 2.3.1 statement
source_evidence.anchor: Let X_i be independent Bernoulli random variables with parameters p_i
source_evidence.observation: The inputs are an indexed finite family of independent Bernoulli variables, with an individual success parameter p_i for each variable.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 7; printed page 18, Theorem 2.3.1 statement
source_evidence.anchor: Consider their sum S_N = sum_{i=1}^N X_i and denote its mean by mu = E S_N
source_evidence.observation: The random quantity controlled is the uncentered sum S_N, and mu denotes the expectation of that sum.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 7; printed page 18, Theorem 2.3.1 displayed conclusion
source_evidence.anchor: Then, for any t > mu, we have P{S_N >= t} <= e^{-mu}(e mu/t)^t
source_evidence.observation: For every threshold strictly above the mean, the upper-tail probability is bounded by the displayed Chernoff expression with exponent t.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 8; printed page 19, proof of Theorem 2.3.1, equation (2.7)
source_evidence.anchor: multiply both sides of the inequality S_N >= t by a parameter lambda, exponentiate, and then use Markov's inequality and independence
source_evidence.observation: For lambda>0 the proof obtains P{S_N>=t} <= e^{-lambda t} product_{i=1}^N E exp(lambda X_i); independence is used to factor the MGF of the sum.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 8; printed page 19, proof of Theorem 2.3.1, Bernoulli MGF computation
source_evidence.anchor: Since X_i takes value 1 with probability p_i and value 0 with probability 1-p_i
source_evidence.observation: The source's Bernoulli convention is {0,1}-valued, and its MGF is e^{lambda}p_i+(1-p_i)=1+(e^{lambda}-1)p_i.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 8; printed page 19, proof of Theorem 2.3.1, product MGF bound
source_evidence.anchor: 1+x <= e^x ... product E exp(lambda X_i) <= exp[(e^{lambda}-1) sum p_i] = exp[(e^{lambda}-1)mu]
source_evidence.observation: The proof identifies mu with sum_i p_i and bounds the product MGF by exp((e^{lambda}-1)mu).

source_evidence.location: PDF page 8; printed page 19, final paragraph of the proof
source_evidence.anchor: This bound holds for any lambda > 0. Substituting the value lambda = ln(t/mu) which is positive by the assumption t > mu
source_evidence.observation: Optimization chooses the natural-log parameter ln(t/mu), yielding the displayed bound when that quotient and logarithm are defined as used.

binders: A finite index bound N and random variables X_1,...,X_N (PDF page 7; printed page 18, Theorem 2.3.1 opening and the displayed definition of S_N).
Bernoulli parameters p_1,...,p_N, one for each X_i (PDF page 7; printed page 18, Theorem 2.3.1 opening).
The sum S_N := sum_{i=1}^N X_i and its mean mu := E S_N (PDF page 7; printed page 18, Theorem 2.3.1 statement).
A threshold t satisfying t>mu (PDF page 7; printed page 18, Theorem 2.3.1 displayed conclusion).
hypotheses: The variables X_i are independent (PDF page 7; printed page 18, Theorem 2.3.1 opening; PDF page 8, printed page 19, derivation of (2.7)).

Each X_i is Bernoulli with its own parameter p_i, meaning it equals 1 with probability p_i and 0 with probability 1-p_i (PDF page 7, printed page 18, theorem opening; PDF page 8, printed page 19, Bernoulli MGF computation).
The tail threshold lies strictly above the sum's mean: t>mu (PDF page 7; printed page 18, theorem conclusion).
conclusions: The upper-tail probability satisfies P{S_N>=t} <= exp(-mu) (e mu/t)^t for every t>mu (PDF page 7; printed page 18, Theorem 2.3.1 displayed bound).
definitions_and_conventions: S_N is the uncentered sum sum_{i=1}^N X_i (PDF page 7; printed page 18, Theorem 2.3.1 statement).
mu is E S_N and, in the proof, equals sum_{i=1}^N p_i (PDF page 7, printed page 18, theorem statement; PDF page 8, printed page 19, product MGF bound).
A Bernoulli(p_i) variable uses the 0/1 convention: probability p_i at 1 and probability 1-p_i at 0 (PDF page 8; printed page 19, Bernoulli MGF paragraph).
The symbols e and ln in the proof are the ordinary exponential base and natural logarithm, as witnessed by exp(lambda X_i), e^lambda, and lambda=ln(t/mu) (PDF page 8; printed page 19, proof).
The probability event is non-strict on the tail side, S_N>=t, while the admissibility condition on t is strict, t>mu (PDF page 7; printed page 18, displayed theorem bound).
implicit_context: The notation X_1,...,X_N and sum from 1 to N treats N as a finite sample count, ordinarily a positive integer, although the theorem does not separately print N>=1 (PDF page 7; printed page 18, theorem statement).

The section introduction contrasts this parameter-sensitive Chernoff bound with the less sensitive general Hoeffding inequality, especially when p_i are small (PDF page 7; printed page 18, Section 2.3 introduction).
The proof reuses the exponential-Markov and independence steps leading to equations (2.5) and (2.6) in the preceding Hoeffding argument (PDF page 8; printed page 19, first proof paragraph).

Because p_i are probabilities under the stated Bernoulli convention, their intended range is 0<=p_i<=1, although this interval is not repeated as a separate hypothesis in the theorem statement (PDF pages 7-8; printed pages 18-19, theorem opening and Bernoulli law expansion).

details: The X_i may have different Bernoulli parameters p_i; identical distribution is not assumed (PDF page 7; printed page 18, theorem opening uses indexed p_i).
The theorem controls the sum S_N itself, not S_N-mu and not an average (PDF page 7; printed page 18, theorem statement and event).
The mean parameter mu is derived from the family as E S_N rather than supplied as an unrelated bound (PDF page 7; printed page 18, theorem statement).
Only the upper tail S_N>=t is asserted in Theorem 2.3.1 (PDF page 7; printed page 18, displayed bound).
The result is stated for every t strictly larger than mu, with no printed restriction that t be an integer even though S_N is integer-valued (PDF page 7; printed page 18, phrase 'for any t>mu').
The right side is the product exp(-mu) times (e mu/t) raised to the threshold t (PDF page 7; printed page 18, displayed theorem formula).
Both occurrences of t are essential: it appears in the denominator of the base and as the exponent (PDF page 7; printed page 18, displayed theorem formula).
For every lambda>0, Markov's inequality and independence give e^{-lambda t} times the product of individual MGFs (PDF page 8; printed page 19, equation (2.7)).
The inequality 1+x<=e^x bounds each Bernoulli MGF and yields exp((e^lambda-1)mu) for the product (PDF page 8; printed page 19, MGF computation).
The source optimizes by lambda=ln(t/mu) (PDF page 8; printed page 19, final proof paragraph).
The printed theorem does not exclude mu=0 (PDF page 7; printed page 18, theorem statement).

The final proof step divides by mu and takes ln(t/mu), so it directly applies only when mu>0; the zero-mean Bernoulli case requires a separate elementary argument or convention (PDF page 8; printed page 19, final proof paragraph).

undebatable_constraints: The variables are independent Bernoulli random variables, not arbitrary bounded variables (PDF page 7; printed page 18, Theorem 2.3.1 opening).
Each variable has its own parameter p_i; equality of the p_i is not required (PDF page 7; printed page 18, theorem opening).
S_N is the finite sum sum_{i=1}^N X_i and mu is exactly E S_N (PDF page 7; printed page 18, theorem statement).
The theorem applies to upper-tail thresholds with t>mu (PDF page 7; printed page 18, theorem statement).
The conclusion is P{S_N>=t} <= exp(-mu)(e mu/t)^t, including the non-strict event boundary (PDF page 7; printed page 18, displayed bound).
The Bernoulli variables take values 0 and 1 with probabilities 1-p_i and p_i respectively (PDF page 8; printed page 19, proof's MGF computation).
Independence is used to factor the MGF across all indices in equation (2.7) (PDF page 8; printed page 19, first proof paragraph and equation (2.7)).

ambiguities.issue: The domain of the threshold t is not stated explicitly.
ambiguities.evidence: The theorem says 'for any t>mu' without declaring t real or integral, while S_N is integer-valued and the proof uses lambda=ln(t/mu) and the real exponent t (PDF pages 7-8; printed pages 18-19).
ambiguities.impact: The proof notation strongly indicates a real threshold, but an exact formal statement must choose the type and real-power convention explicitly.

ambiguities.issue: The zero-mean Bernoulli case is included by the printed hypotheses but not covered by the displayed optimization step.
ambiguities.evidence: No hypothesis states mu>0, yet the proof substitutes lambda=ln(t/mu) (PDF page 7, printed page 18, theorem statement; PDF page 8, printed page 19, final proof paragraph).
ambiguities.impact: When mu=0 and t>0, every p_i is zero and the upper-tail probability is zero, so the result has an elementary degenerate proof; nevertheless an exact formalization must split this case or add a positivity hypothesis, and must specify the meaning of the right side at zero.

ambiguities.issue: Positivity of the finite count N is only conventional, not separately stated.
ambiguities.evidence: The theorem writes X_1,...,X_N and sum_{i=1}^N but gives no explicit N>=1 condition (PDF page 7; printed page 18, theorem statement).
ambiguities.impact: An exact finite-index formalization must decide whether the empty family is included; if included, it falls into the same mu=0 boundary case.

contract_plain_english: Let X_1 through X_N be independent, not necessarily identically distributed, 0/1 Bernoulli variables with success probabilities p_i. Write S_N for their sum and mu for its expectation, equivalently the sum of the p_i. For every threshold t strictly above mu, the probability that S_N is at least t is at most exp(-mu) times (e mu/t)^t. The proof factors the exponential moment by independence, bounds each Bernoulli MGF using 1+x<=e^x, and optimizes at lambda=ln(t/mu). The source leaves the type of t and the empty/zero-mean boundary implicit; the stated result includes mu=0, but that case needs a separate argument because the printed optimizer divides by mu.
